subject: Michael Jordan vs. His Era

facts.text: Most regular-season points in the NBA from 1984-85 through 1997-98: Jordan, 29,277. Next: Karl Malone, 27,782 — 1,495 behind.
facts.why: Answers "who owned the era" with one number, and the gap to No. 2 is the hook.

facts.text: Most playoff points in the NBA from 1984-85 through 1997-98: Jordan, 5,987. Next: Karl Malone, 3,691 — 2,296 behind.
facts.why: Answers "who owned the era" with one number, and the gap to No. 2 is the hook.

facts.text: Seasons averaging 30 points from 1984-85 through 1997-98: Jordan 8 (1986-87, 1987-88, 1988-89, 1989-90, 1990-91, 1991-92, 1992-93, 1995-96); everyone else combined 4 (Bernard King, Dominique Wilkins and Karl Malone).
facts.why: "Him vs the whole league" is the most shareable Jordan frame, and the lopsided count proves it.

facts.text: Postseasons of 10+ games averaging 30 points from 1984-85 through 1997-98: Jordan 10 (1987-88, 1988-89, 1989-90, 1990-91, 1991-92, 1992-93, 1994-95, 1995-96, 1996-97, 1997-98); everyone else combined 4 (Alex English, Dominique Wilkins, Hakeem Olajuwon and Shaquille O'Neal).
facts.why: Playoff scoring is the core of the GOAT debate; the count against the field is stark.

facts.text: Best regular-season scoring average from 1984-85 through 1997-98 (400+ games): Jordan, 31.5 — next Shaquille O'Neal, 27.2. Top five: Michael Jordan 31.5, Shaquille O'Neal 27.2, Dominique Wilkins 26.4, Karl Malone 26.2, Larry Bird 25.6.
facts.why: The top-five list names his rivals, so every fan base in it shares or argues with it.

facts.text: Best playoff scoring average from 1984-85 through 1997-98 (50+ games): Jordan, 33.4 — next Hakeem Olajuwon, 27.0. Top five: Michael Jordan 33.4, Hakeem Olajuwon 27.0, Karl Malone 26.9, Shaquille O'Neal 26.7, Larry Bird 24.4.
facts.why: The top-five list names his rivals, so every fan base in it shares or argues with it.

facts.text: Best playoff steals average from 1984-85 through 1997-98 (50+ games): Jordan, 2.10 — next Isiah Thomas, 2.08. Top five: Michael Jordan 2.10, Isiah Thomas 2.08, Clyde Drexler 1.95, Scottie Pippen 1.93, John Stockton 1.89.
facts.why: The top-five list names his rivals, so every fan base in it shares or argues with it.

facts.text: 2,500-point seasons from 1984-85 through 1997-98: Jordan 6 (1986-87, 1987-88, 1988-89, 1989-90, 1990-91, 1992-93); everyone else combined 1 (Karl Malone).
facts.why: A round-number club he nearly owned outright.

facts.text: Seasons averaging 30 points on 50% shooting from 1984-85 through 1997-98: Jordan 5 (1987-88, 1988-89, 1989-90, 1990-91, 1991-92); everyone else combined 2 (Bernard King and Karl Malone).
facts.why: Kills the "volume shooter" argument with efficiency and volume together.

facts.text: Seasons with 2,000 points and 200 steals from 1984-85 through 1997-98: Jordan 6 (1986-87, 1987-88, 1988-89, 1989-90, 1990-91, 1992-93); everyone else combined 3 (Clyde Drexler and Hakeem Olajuwon).
facts.why: Scorer and ball-hawk in one line; the two-way case in a single stat.

facts.text: Seasons averaging 30 points and 2.5 steals from 1984-85 through 1997-98: Jordan 6 (1986-87, 1987-88, 1988-89, 1989-90, 1990-91, 1992-93); everyone else combined 0.
facts.why: An exclusive two-way club; the empty 'everyone else' side is the post.

facts.text: Postseasons of 10+ games averaging 30 points on 50% shooting from 1984-85 through 1997-98: Jordan 4 (1987-88, 1988-89, 1989-90, 1990-91); everyone else combined 3 (Alex English, Hakeem Olajuwon and Shaquille O'Neal).
facts.why: Big-game efficiency is the rebuttal to every "he took too many shots" take.

facts.text: Jordan led the NBA in field goals made 10 times: 1986-87 (1,098; next Alex English 965); 1987-88 (1,069; next Dominique Wilkins 909); 1988-89 (966; next Alex English 924); 1989-90 (1,034; next Patrick Ewing 922); 1990-91 (990; next Karl Malone 847); 1991-92 (943; next Chris Mullin 830); 1992-93 (992; next Hakeem Olajuwon 848); 1995-96 (916; next Karl Malone 789); 1996-97 (920; next Karl Malone 864); 1997-98 (881; next Karl Malone 780).
facts.why: 10 field-goal titles is a stat almost nobody knows; the runner-up names add rival fan bases.

facts.text: Playoffs vs. Detroit: 4 series (1-3), 22 games, 10-12, 30.0 points a game.
facts.why: The Bad Boys rivalry in numbers; Pistons and Bulls fans both engage.

facts.text: Most regular-season field goals in the NBA from 1984-85 through 1997-98: Jordan, 10,962. Next: Karl Malone, 10,290 — 672 behind.
facts.why: Made baskets, not just shots: the volume answer to "he just shot a lot".

facts.text: Most regular-season field-goal attempts in the NBA from 1984-85 through 1997-98: Jordan, 21,686. Next: Karl Malone, 19,504 — 2,182 behind.
facts.why: Leans into the volume critique and owns it; sparks replies either way.

facts.text: Most playoff field goals in the NBA from 1984-85 through 1997-98: Jordan, 2,188. Next: Hakeem Olajuwon, 1,469 — 719 behind.
facts.why: Made baskets, not just shots: the volume answer to "he just shot a lot".

facts.text: Most playoff free throws made in the NBA from 1984-85 through 1997-98: Jordan, 1,463. Next: Karl Malone, 1,002 — 461 behind.
facts.why: Getting to the line was half his game; this is the number that shows it.

facts.text: Most playoff steals in the NBA from 1984-85 through 1997-98: Jordan, 376. Next: Scottie Pippen, 344 — 32 behind.
facts.why: Defense in the biggest games; his running mate is right behind him, which Pippen fans love.

facts.text: Most playoff minutes in the NBA from 1984-85 through 1997-98: Jordan, 7,474. Next: Scottie Pippen, 7,028 — 446 behind.
facts.why: Playoff minutes measure how deep his teams went, year after year.
Raw shot-making volume that the three-point era rarely approaches; great for then-vs-now debates.

facts.text: Seasons averaging 25 points, 6 rebounds and 6 assists from 1984-85 through 1997-98: Jordan 3 (1988-89, 1989-90, 1991-92); everyone else combined 5 (Larry Bird and Clyde Drexler).
facts.why: All-around production framing that pulls Magic, Bird and LeBron-era comparisons into the replies.

facts.text: 600-point postseasons from 1984-85 through 1997-98: Jordan 3 (1991-92, 1992-93, 1997-98); everyone else combined 4 (Larry Bird, Charles Barkley and Hakeem Olajuwon).
facts.why: Deep-run scoring volume; ties directly to the titles.

facts.text: Jordan led the NBA in total points in 11 of the 14 seasons from 1984-85 through 1997-98; the others went to Alex English (1985-86), David Robinson (1993-94) and Shaquille O'Neal (1994-95).
facts.why: Total points (not average) removes the games-played asterisk; naming the other leaders makes it trivia.

facts.text: Seasons in which Jordan and Scottie Pippen both averaged 20 points: 3 — 1991-92 (30.1 and 21.0), 1994-95 (26.9 and 21.4; Jordan played 17 games) and 1996-97 (29.6 and 20.2).
facts.why: Duo content always travels; the small number surprises people who remember them as co-stars every year.

facts.text: Jordan reached 25,000 regular-season points in his 782nd game, Nov 30, 1996 at San Antonio.
facts.why: Reached in his second Bulls stint, after the baseball break; a comeback-chapter milestone.

facts.text: Jordan reached 30,000 regular-season points in his 960th game, Jan 4, 2002 vs. Chicago.
facts.why: Reached against the Bulls in a Wizards uniform; the irony makes it a story.

facts.text: Jordan reached 32,000 regular-season points in his 1,059th game, Mar 23, 2003 at Golden State.
facts.why: His final milestone, at 40; longevity content.

facts.text: Christmas Day: 6 regular-season games, 28.3 points a game, 5-1 — 30 at New York 1986; 37 vs. Detroit 1990; 14 vs. Boston 1991; 42 vs. New York 1992; 23 vs. Detroit 1996; 24 vs. Miami 1997.
facts.why: Seasonal hook: post it on Christmas when the league's showcase games are on.

facts.text: On his birthday (Feb. 17) he played 4 regular-season games: 26 at Milwaukee in 1985; 46 vs. Cleveland in 1992; 27 vs. Utah in 1993; 27 vs. Indiana in 1998.
facts.why: Post it every Feb. 17; birthday content for the biggest name in the sport is guaranteed reach.

facts.text: In the 30 games that clinched a playoff series he averaged 33.9 points.
facts.why: Closer framing across every round, not just the Finals.

facts.text: 700-free-throw seasons from 1984-85 through 1997-98: Jordan 2 (1986-87, 1987-88); everyone else combined 3 (Moses Malone, Charles Barkley and Karl Malone).
facts.why: Shows how often he lived at the line, an underrated part of his scoring.

facts.text: Seasons averaging 40 minutes and 30 points from 1984-85 through 1997-98: Jordan 3 (1986-87, 1987-88, 1988-89); everyone else combined 0.
facts.why: Workload angle: fans compare it with today's load management.

facts.text: 1984-85: Jordan was 3rd in scoring at 28.2, behind Bernard King (32.9) and Larry Bird (28.7).
facts.why: Rookie-year context: who was ahead of him before the run of titles began.

facts.text: 1987-88 scoring title: Jordan 35.0, runner-up Dominique Wilkins 30.7 — a margin of 4.3 a game.

facts.text: 1988-89 scoring title: Jordan 32.5, runner-up Karl Malone 29.1 — a margin of 3.4 a game.

facts.text: 1988-89 playoffs: most points of anyone, 591 in 17 games (34.8); next James Worthy, 372.

facts.text: 1989-90 scoring title: Jordan 33.6, runner-up Karl Malone 31.0 — a margin of 2.6 a game.

method: Michael Jordan vs. his era: every line is computed from stats.nba.com — each player-season of 1984-85 through 1997-98 (and 2001-03 where noted) and every game Jordan played. Nothing typed in from memory.

Era leaderboards sum each player's seasons across the span; per-game leaderboards require the stated minimum games. Scoring titles use the rule of his era: 70 games or 1,400 points. 'Why' notes are editorial: why the line should work as a post.
